13. Mr Khan then turns his attention on the merit of the appeal and submits that the trial Court on consideration of the pleadings, the evidence adduced by the parties and taking into consideration the materials on record rightly found that the plaintiffs have complied with the formalities of Talab-i-Muw-sibat and Talab-i-Ishhad within the meaning of the Muslim Law. in elaborating his argument on this point, he submits that the plaintiff No. 2 has performed those formalities for and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 and on his behalf though at the time of deposition he stated that he made the Talabs for pre-empting the properties under the Muslim Law and there is no discrepancy in the evidence of PWs. The learned Advocate for the respondent submits that there is no specific form for performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat though certain formalities have been laid down for the performance of Talab-i-Ishhad and from the deposition of PW 1 it becomes clear that the specific intention for pre-empting the suit land by the plaintiffs have been expressed on 9--1997 by performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat on the suit land. Mr Khan further submitted that it does not lie in the mouth of the appellant to say that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their ownership in the 'B' Schedule land, inasmuch as the DWs in one voice admitted in their evidence that to the contiguous south of the suit land, the land of the plaintiffs are situated. Mr Khan submitted that there is sufficient oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs stating that they are the purchaser of 'B' Schedule land and the certified copies of the deeds in question have been exhibited by the plaintiffs before the trial Court and the original title deeds could not be produced as they are lying with the Bank. In elaborating his submission he further submits that besides the PWs the DWs also admitted that the plaintiffs are the owner of the 'B' Schedule land and the legal position is that things admitted need not be proved. There-fore, even in the absence of any evidence the trial Court is justified in arriving at a finding that the plaintiffs are the real owner of the 'B' Schedule land and thereby the first pre-requisite for filing of the suit for pre-emption by the plaintiffs have been fulfilled. Mr Khan further submitted that Mr Tabarak Hussain forcefully argued that the suit lands are not agricultural land and are commercial plots, but this submission is contrary to material and evidence on record. Exhibits 5(Kha) and 3 (Gha) i.e. Khatian and rent receipt, as well as the title deeds of the defendant No. 1 show that the suit land is agricultural land and the 'B' Schedule land is Chala land and Chala land is also agricultural land within the meaning of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951. Therefore, it cannot be said that the lands in question are commercial plots and therefore, cannot be a subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. Mr Khan further submitted that to prove the ownership of the 'B' Schedule land the plaintiffs produced and exhibited current rent receipts which have been admitted without any objection and it is now well settled that khatian and rent receipts are documents of possession and collateral documents of title as has been laid down in 35 DLR (AD) 216. Mr Khan further submitted that it has been contended by the appellants that the plaintiffs did not make the Talab-i-Ishhad promptly but there is no basis for that as admitted facts show that the plaintiffs first came to know about the sale in question on 9-3-1997 and on the next date sent their man to the local Registry Office and obtained the certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 when the plaintiffs acquired a definite know-ledge as to the sale of the suit lands by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 to the defendant No. 1 and then on 19-3-1997 made Talab-i-Ishhad. Mr Enayet Hossain Khan in the course of argument also submitted that in a suit for pre-emption the plaintiffs need not establish their title, inasmuch as the title of the plaintiffs is not in issue and it has been categorically stated by the plaintiffs in their plaint that they are owner by purchase of the 'B' Schedule land which has not been denied by the defendants in their written statement. Therefore, it must be presumed that the defendants have admitted the aforesaid statement of the plaintiffs and now they cannot resale from that and take a different stand giving a go-by to the earlier stand. Mr Khan also submitted that the trial Court has rightly taken the view that the boundary wall erected in between the 'A' and 'B' Schedule lands cannot stand in the way of the plaintiffs to get an order of pre-emption in their favour inasmuch as the 'B' Schedule land is contiguous to 'A' Schedule land. 

 14. Mr Hossain has intensively and extensively argued about the constitutionality of the law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage, i.e. the right to pre-empt as a 'Shafi-i-Jar i.e. as owner of adjacent immovable property. It appears that the question of void ness of Shafi-i-Jar has not been agitated before our Court until now though the point has been urged before the Indian jurisdiction in 1962 and the same question also came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Initially, in the Indian jurisdiction there was difference of opinion at the High Court level as to whether right of pre-emption based on vicinage is constitutional or not and that controversy has been set at rest by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Bhauram vs Bhijnath AIR 1962 (SC) 1476 and the case of Saint vs Labh Singh reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 314. It has been held by the Indian Supreme Court that a statutory or a cautionary right of pre-emption based on vicinage is unconstitutional as it imposes un-reasonable restriction upon the right to acquire property as guaranteed to a citizen in India under Article 19(1)(f) of the Indian Constitution but the Indian Supreme Court, however, upheld the validity of such a right based on co-ownership and on certain appendages, such as a common stair and a common entrance. As against that the position in Pakistan is that the question of constitutionality of law of pre-emption under Muslim Law came up for consideration in the case of Allah Box vs Jano and others reported in PLD 1962 (WP) Karachi 317. In that case it was argued that the law of pre-emption is in conflict with Article 11 of the late Constitution of Pakistan and, as such, it was not a valid law. The Karachi High Court following the decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court which is reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 533 = 11 DLR (SC) 1, i.e. the case of State vs Doss and another, held that the law of pre-emption as applicable to that part of the Province was in operation and therefore, held that it was wrong on the part of the appellant's Counsel to say that the law of pre-emption was no longer in force. Their Lordships of the Karachi High Court negative the contention that the law of pre-emption comes into conflict with Article 11 of the Constitution on the ground that at that time there was no fundamental right in force under the Marital Law regime as the chapter of fundamental rights in which Article 11 occurs, having, according to their Lordships of the Supreme Court, disappeared from the "new legal order", the argument advanced by the learned Counsel is not available to him and on that count the law of pre-emption was upheld. It thus appears that in Pakistan the question was raised at a point of time when the citizens had no fundamental rights guaranteed to them as the Constitution was abrogated. But after returning to Constitutional Rule the question does not appear to have been re-agitated. So far Bangladesh is concerned, it appears that the constitutionality of right of pre-emption based on vicinage either under the Muslim Law or under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951 has not been called in question and it is only in this case that Mr Hussain has urged this point for the first time. 

 16. During the British rule in Bengal Muslim Law was applied among the Muslims and for the first time by incorporating section 26F in Bengal Tenancy Act, 1882 the provision for pre-emption was introduced for all citizens irrespective of caste or creed and that concept of pre-emption is borrowed from the Muslim law of Shafi-i-Sharik and Shafi-i-Jar but no such provision was available to the non-Muslims for pre-empting any sale of urban property. It is only after the coming into force of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 the non-Muslims could also exercise their right of pre-emption in respect of town property. Thus, an anomaly existed in undivided Bengal during the British regime. A Muslim could exercise right of pre-emption both in respect of urban and agricultural properties whereas a non-Muslim could only exercise their right of pre-emption in respect of agricultural properties until 1949. There was another discrepancy. The limitation for instituting a suit under section 26F was 3 years whereas limitation for pre-emption under Muslim Law was and is one year as provided by Article 10 of the Limitation Act. Besides, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, in order to pre-empt a sale, the pre-emptor has to pay an amount to the extent of 10% or 5% above the consideration as the case may be. Thus, a citizen other than a Muslim is worse off in initiating a pre-emption proceedings under the general law, whereas under the Muslim law no such amount is required to be deposited in the Court.

 18. A combined reading of the aforesaid sections clearly indicate that so far it relates to agricultural land both the Muslims as well as non-Muslims, i.e. all citizens of Bangladesh, stand at par. In case of a non-Muslim he can invoke his right under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act whereas a Muslim citizen can invoke his right of pre-emption either under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under the Muslim Law. Only difference is that if he resorts to Muslim law he has a limitation of one year whereas limitation under section 96 is for 120 days from the date of knowledge. So far it relates to non-agricultural land, a Muslim can enforce his right of pre-emption either under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act or under the Muslim Law whereas a Non-Muslim can only resort to the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act only a co-sharer in land can initiate a proceeding but under the Muslim Law contiguous land owner can also avail the opportunity. It, therefore, appears that the Muslim Law of pre-emption is applicable to both agricultural and non-agricultural lands and the non-Muslim citizen is likely to be worse off in the case of non-agricultural land as he has a shorter period of limitation and he is also to pay 5% more above the sale price. In Article 28(1) it has been laid down that the State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. It, thus, appears that Muslim Law of pre-emption so far it is applicable to the urban property is discriminatory and a Muslim citizen is placed at a higher plain than the other non-Muslim citizens of the State and this also affects the secular nature of the Republic. We are, therefore, of the opinion that Muslim law of pre-emption so far it relates to the town property is void on the ground that it discriminates between a citizen and a citizen on the ground of religion and faith, inasmuch as under section 24 of the Act a non-Muslim contiguous land holder cannot maintain an action for pre-emption but a Muslim can.
